question: Why do AI chatbots sometimes make things up, and what are two ways to reduce it?
reference_answer: Made-up answers (hallucinations) arise from factors such as noisy data, model overconfidence, lack of knowledge and the generation process itself. Two ways to reduce them are faithful finetuning, which models hallucination explicitly, and giving the model retrieved context from external sources (shown in a medical question-answering system).
notes: plain. Needs two abstracts: causes of hallucination and faithful finetuning from 2406.11267, retrieved context as mitigation from 2409.10011. A deliberately general plain multi-hop item; other papers in the full index may also answer (see pooling rule 9).
author: LDN

question: Is it always better to give an AI more retrieved documents when it answers a question?
reference_answer: No. For many long-context models, answer quality first improves and then declines as more passages are retrieved, because retrieved "hard negatives" (irrelevant passages) hurt.
notes: plain. Answer is in the abstract of 2410.05983. Other papers may say similar things (see the pooling rule in FORMAT.md).
author: LDN

question: Do large language models know when to hold back instead of answering a medical question?
reference_answer: Often not. In one study of five frontier models, on medical QA questions where the correct option had been removed, the models still picked an answer at high rates (false-action rates of 55-81% on MedQA and 53-82% on AfriMed-QA). Safety-oriented prompting reduced this but residual failure persisted.
notes: plain. The question names the setting (medical questions) because the evidence is one study (rule 10). Answer is in the abstract of 2605.15000. Related to the refusal behaviour we measure in RQ2.
author: LDN

question: What is the difference between checking an answer by matching words and checking it by meaning?
reference_answer: Word-overlap metrics such as ROUGE, METEOR and exact match miss semantic equivalence. Semantic metrics (BERTScore, MoverScore, cross-encoder models) compare meaning and correlate better with human judgement when there is no lexical overlap; SMILE combines both kinds.
notes: plain. Comparison across two abstracts on QA answer evaluation.
author: LDN

question: In RAG, how does the chunk size affect answer quality, and can chunks at several levels (multi-sentence, paragraph, section, document) do better than one level?
reference_answer: In one study, answer quality depends on the chunk size: an optimal size balances enough context against irrelevant information. A multi-level approach (chunks at multi-sentence, paragraph, section and document level) improved AI-evaluated answer correctness by 25.739% over single-level RAG on Glycoscience papers.
notes: plain. Relevant to our own chunking choice. Two abstracts: 2407.19794 for the optimal chunk size, 2501.16952 for multiple abstraction levels. The question names the multi-level approach (rule 10).
author: LDN

question: How can a token-level hallucination detector for RAG use the retrieved documents to find ungrounded tokens?
reference_answer: It compares the model's internal representations with and without the retrieved documents, on the idea that grounded tokens are more influenced by the documents than hallucinated ones. It also uses how document information propagates through preceding tokens and applies span smoothing.
notes: expert. Uses RAG and token-level terms; the question says "a detector", and the answer is the method of one paper. Answer is in the abstract of 2606.31033.
author: LDN

question: Name two approaches that detect hallucination from a language model's internal states instead of its output text.
reference_answer: One audits LLM activations with weakly supervised subset scanning to find anomalous patterns such as hallucinations. Another (CORTEX) compares internal representations with and without retrieved documents to flag ungrounded tokens in RAG outputs.
notes: expert. Needs two abstracts; neither names the other. The question asks for two approaches, because other internal-state detectors in the full index would also be correct (rule 10).
author: LDN

question: Is there a single score that combines calibration, robustness and uncertainty to measure how reliable an LLM is?
reference_answer: The Composite Reliability Score (CRS) integrates calibration, robustness and uncertainty quantification into a single interpretable metric; it was tested on ten open-source LLMs across five QA datasets.
notes: expert. Technical wording; the abstract names the score and what it integrates, not how (no formula). Answer in the abstract of 2512.24058.
author: LDN

question: What is In-Context RALM, and why is it easier to deploy than other retrieval-augmented language models?
reference_answer: In-Context RALM leaves the language model unchanged and simply prepends retrieved grounding documents to the input, with no extra training. Other retrieval-augmented approaches modify the model architecture, which complicates deployment; this one works with off-the-shelf retrievers, and could be used even when the model is only reachable through an API.
notes: specific. Names the method. Answer is in the abstract of 2302.00083, and the idea matches how our own system supplies retrieved chunks to the LLM.
author: LDN

question: How much better is LongRAG than ordinary RAG and long-context LLMs on multi-hop question answering over long documents?
reference_answer: On three multi-hop datasets, LongRAG outperforms long-context LLMs by up to 6.94%, advanced RAG by 6.16% and vanilla RAG by 17.25%.
notes: specific. Names the method; three numbers in the abstract of 2410.18050.
author: LDN

question: Does the way a prompt is laid out, for example as plain text, Markdown or JSON, change how well a GPT model does the task?
reference_answer: Yes. In one study, GPT-3.5-turbo's performance varied by up to 40% on a code translation task depending on the prompt template (plain text, Markdown, JSON or YAML), while the larger GPT-4 was more robust to these changes.
notes: plain. Answer is in the abstract of 2411.10541 (the 40% figure and the GPT-4 robustness).
author: LDN

question: How much does ShotKV improve accuracy on long-context generation tasks, and how much latency does it save compared with running with the full cache?
reference_answer: ShotKV improves accuracy by 9%-18% on long-context generation tasks and reduces latency by 11% compared with full cache inference.
notes: specific. Names the method. Both numbers are in the abstract of 2502.01941.
author: LDN

question: Can preference tuning on English data alone make a multilingual language model less toxic in other languages?
reference_answer: In one study, yes: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with only English data greatly reduced toxic output in 17 languages (for mGPT-1.3B, the chance of a toxic continuation fell from 46.8% to 3.9%). The authors explain it by a dual multilinguality property of the MLP layers, and they found that bilingual sentence retrieval can predict how well the effect transfers to a language.
notes: expert. Answer is in the abstract of 2406.16235. The question says "can" and does not claim that every method works.
author: LDN

question: Does the order of the answer choices change how well an AI model does on a multiple-choice test?
reference_answer: Yes. In one study of instruction-tuned language models on four multiple-choice benchmarks, performance dropped noticeably when the order of the choices was changed, which points to a selection (positional) bias toward the first positions. Asking the model to reason step by step with Chain-of-Thought reduced the bias and made the models more robust.
notes: plain. Answer is in the abstract of 2309.12481 (order bias, first-position preference, Chain-of-Thought mitigation).
author: LDN

question: Why can an AI judge give misleading quality scores, and how can a small number of human labels be used to correct them?
reference_answer: Two studies point to different problems. In Tang poetry generation, LLM judges systematically overrated machine-written poems that copy statistical patterns but break prosodic rules, which differed from expert judgments. In factuality evaluation, judge-predicted scores underestimated the human-annotated accuracy; combining judge predictions on the whole dataset with human labels on a small, strategically chosen subset gives statistically valid estimates, and choosing that subset with failure-space analysis improved annotation efficiency over uniform or uncertainty-based sampling.
notes: expert. Needs both abstracts: 2510.15313 for the judge problem (the "echo chamber" effect) and 2609.00494 for the human-anchored correction. Other papers may also answer (see pooling rule 9).
author: LDN

question: How does SetFit differ from LoRA fine-tuning of a large language model when you want to train a text classifier with limited data and hardware?
reference_answer: SetFit fine-tunes a small Sentence Transformer on a few text pairs in a contrastive way and then trains a classification head on the embeddings; it needs no prompts and orders of magnitude fewer parameters than existing techniques, and it trains an order of magnitude faster than PEFT and PET. LoRA and QLoRA instead adapt an instruction-tuned large language model by training fewer than 1% of its parameters, which allowed experiments on a single consumer-grade GPU (shown on 50,281 annotated Bengali comments for hate speech detection). The abstracts describe the two methods; they do not compare them with each other.
notes: specific. Names both methods. Comparison across two abstracts: 2209.11055 (SetFit) and 2510.16985 (LoRA/QLoRA on one consumer GPU).
author: LDN

question: How does high-precision scoring fix the problem of tied relevance scores when a retrieval system runs in low precision?
reference_answer: In low precision, relevance scores lose granularity, which creates spurious ties whose resolution changes the metrics. High-Precision Scoring (HPS) casts only the final scoring step to a higher precision, which resolves tied candidates at minimal extra cost and dramatically reduces the instability caused by ties. The paper pairs it with Tie-aware Retrieval Metrics (TRM), which report the expected score, the range and the bias caused by the order of tied candidates.
notes: specific. Names the method and the problem. Answer is in the abstract of 2508.03306.
author: LDN

question: Can you tell it not to?
reference_answer: It helps: in one study, directly instructing ChatGPT to give outputs that comply with privacy rules such as HIPAA and GDPR led to a significant omission of personally identifiable information from the output.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that "it" is the chatbot's copying of personal details. The answer is in the abstract of 2305.15008, which reports a significant omission of personal information, not that copying stops.
author: LDN

history.content: Do chatbots repeat the personal details I put in a prompt?
They can. In one study, ChatGPT kept personally identifiable information word for word in 57.4% of its summaries of 100 cover letters.

standalone_query: Can ChatGPT be instructed to leave personal information out of its output to comply with privacy rules such as HIPAA and GDPR?

question: What goes wrong with those methods?
reference_answer: Test-time scaling methods such as Beam Search and DVTS often suffer from path homogenization (the reasoning paths become too similar) and from inefficient use of intermediate results.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know which methods are meant. The answer is in the abstract of 2505.17829, which proposes SRCA to fix these two limitations.
author: LDN

history.content: How can a language model get better at maths problems by using more computation at answer time?
One family of ways is test-time scaling, such as Beam Search and DVTS, which spend more computation at inference to improve accuracy on step-by-step mathematical reasoning.

standalone_query: What are the limitations of test-time scaling methods such as Beam Search and DVTS for mathematical reasoning?

question: How can a system route questions to different language models while respecting each user's own balance between cost and quality?
reference_answer: One approach, MetaRouter, treats each user's cost-performance preference as a separate task in a contextual bandit and uses meta-learning so that it learns the user's implicit preference from very little interaction, then sends each query to the most suitable model.
notes: plain. Answer is in the abstract of 2606.06178. The question says "how can" and the answer says "one approach" (rule 10).
author: LDN

question: How many parameters does GPT-4 have, according to papers that report a figure?
reference_answer: The two papers do not agree on one number. A review of GPT-4 says its model size is larger than GPT-3's, "more than one trillion" parameters, while a study that compares ChatGPT-4 with humans on grammaticality judgements lists ChatGPT-4 at 1.5 trillion.
notes: plain. Two abstracts that give different figures: 2305.03195 (review of GPT-4) and 2404.14883 (grammaticality study). Found by FAO in the full corpus (snapshot 307); both abstracts were read on arXiv. Not in the 1,000-record sample. A conflicting-evidence item: the answer must report both figures.
author: LDN

question: Does that work equally well for every kind of task?
reference_answer: No. In one empirical study of speculative decoding, the type of task predicted whether draft tokens were accepted better than their depth in the token tree, and only the chat domain consistently gave an expected accepted length above one token per step (the other domains were code generation, mathematical reasoning and logical reasoning).
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that "that" is speculative decoding. The answer is in the abstract of 2604.14682, which reports task type as a stronger predictor of acceptance than tree depth.
author: LDN

history.content: How can I make a large language model generate text faster without changing what it says?
One way is speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes several upcoming tokens and the larger model checks them in a single pass.

standalone_query: Does the acceptance of draft tokens in speculative decoding depend on the type of task?

question: Can the model be protected against that without retraining it?
reference_answer: One approach is Dynamic Deep Prompt Optimization (DDPO). It uses the model's own intermediate layers to generate defensive embeddings with a lightweight multilayer perceptron and injects them into a later layer, so the defence depends on the input and the model's weights are not changed.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that "that" is a jailbreak attack. The answer is in the abstract of 2609.26185, which proposes DDPO as a defence that does not modify the model weights.
author: LDN

history.content: What is a jailbreak attack on a chatbot?
It is an attack that makes a language model produce harmful or unintended content.

standalone_query: How can a language model be protected against jailbreak attacks without fine-tuning it?

question: Is there one best setting for every task?
reference_answer: No. In one study that tested temperatures from 0 to 2 on data sets for six capabilities, the effect of temperature differed by skill, so the best value depends on the task. The authors propose a BERT-based selector that picks a temperature for each prompt, which improved small and medium models on SuperGLUE.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that "setting" is the sampling temperature. The answer is in the abstract of 2506.07295, which reports skill-specific effects of temperature.
author: LDN

history.content: What does the temperature setting do when a language model writes text?
It controls how random the output is: the temperature reshapes the probability distribution over the next token.

standalone_query: Is there a single best sampling temperature for all tasks of a large language model?

question: What have researchers done about gender bias in Chinese text and in machine translation?
reference_answer: For Chinese, one team detected, classified and mitigated sentence-level gender bias by fine-tuning large language models with LoRA, balancing the training data, voting over several expert models and sampling at multiple temperatures. For translation into genderless languages, the Translate-with-Care dataset (3,950 scenarios, six languages) showed that models such as GPT-4 and Google Translate prefer masculine pronouns when stereotypes can influence the choice, and fine-tuning mBART-50 on it substantially resolved these biases.
notes: plain. Needs both papers: 2509.07889 for Chinese detection and mitigation, 2506.00748 for bias in translation. The question names no method, so any paper on either part may also fit (rule 9).
author: LDN

question: How can you tell whether a text was part of a language model's training data: by testing the model, or by searching the training corpus?
reference_answer: VeilProbe tests a black-box model using only its input and output texts: it learns the mapping from a text to the model's generated continuation, perturbs key tokens and classifies membership automatically. Koala takes the other route: a searchable index over a pre-training corpus (the public part of OPT 175B's data), used to measure overlap with benchmarks and the memorization in model output.
notes: plain. Needs both abstracts: 2506.19399 (VeilProbe, black-box membership detection) and 2303.14770 (Koala, corpus index). Each abstract describes one route.
author: LDN

question: How many parameters does the OLMoE language model use for each token, and how much data was it trained on?
reference_answer: OLMoE-1B-7B has 7 billion parameters in total but uses only 1 billion per input token, and it was pretrained on 5 trillion tokens.
notes: specific. Names the model. The answer is in the abstract of 2409.02060.
author: LDN

question: How can a language model be made cheaper to run in one specialised domain by changing its vocabulary?
reference_answer: In one approach, AdaptiVocab, tokens are replaced with domain-specific n-gram-based tokens, so fewer tokens are needed for both input and output. The new token embeddings are initialised from an exponentially weighted combination of existing embeddings and a lightweight fine-tuning on a single GPU follows. On two 7B models across three niche domains it cut token usage by over 25% without hurting performance.
notes: plain. The answer is in the abstract of 2503.19693. Other papers on vocabulary adaptation may say related things (rule 9).
author: LDN

question: Do language models get better at knowing when they are wrong as they are trained or as they get larger?
reference_answer: Not in one study of pre-trained language models, which varied training steps and model scale among other factors: they do not learn to become calibrated during training, because their confidence keeps rising whether or not the predictions are correct. This partly contradicts two common assumptions, that larger models are more calibrated and that pretraining improves calibration.
notes: plain. The answer is in the abstract of 2211.00151, which studies calibration during training and with model scale.
author: LDN

question: How can a question that depends on earlier turns of a conversation be rewritten to stand on its own, and can this be learned without human-labelled data?
reference_answer: Conversational query rewriting turns a conversational query into a self-contained utterance, so a multi-turn problem becomes a single-turn one. In one study, a Transformer model called Teresa was trained on a large dataset built automatically by self-supervised learning, with no human annotation, and used keyword detection and an intent-consistency constraint; it outperformed existing rewriting baselines.
notes: plain. The answer is in the abstract of 2102.04708, which also matches the query-rewriting step of our own agent.
author: LDN

question: How much revenue did OpenAI make from its API last year?
reference_answer: No abstract in the corpus reports a company's revenue from its language-model API; research abstracts do not contain private financial figures.
notes: plain. Topic looks related (LLM providers) but asks for a private company figure that no research abstract gives. To be confirmed with a full-corpus search (rule 7).
author: LDN

question: Which language model will have the highest MMLU score in 2027?
reference_answer: No abstract can answer this: it asks for a future result, and the corpus only contains work published up to its snapshot.
notes: plain. A forecast, so unanswerable by design, but phrased like a benchmark question. To be confirmed with a full-corpus search (rule 7).
author: LDN

question: A method that keeps attention entropy stable by changing the rotary position embedding base and scaling the attention logits can stretch LLaMA-2-7B-Chat to a 16K-token context; how much fine-tuning does it need?
reference_answer: Very little: 100 training samples and 6 training steps are enough to extend the context window of LLaMA-2-7B-Chat to 16,384 tokens.
notes: specific. Names the method by what it does. Answer is in the abstract of 2401.07004 (100 samples, 6 steps, 16,384 tokens).
author: LDN

question: How accurate is BERT-Large when it is pretrained with differentially private SGD in very large batches, compared with ordinary BERT?
reference_answer: The differentially private model reaches a masked language model accuracy of 60.5% at a batch size of 2M with epsilon = 5.36, while non-private BERT models reach about 70%.
notes: specific. Names the setting (BERT-Large, DP-SGD, mega-batches). Answer is in the abstract of 2108.01624; the paper is from 2021.
author: LDN

question: Where do the claims in the MultiFC fact-checking dataset come from, and how well does the best model predict whether a claim is true?
reference_answer: The claims come from 26 English fact-checking websites and were labelled for veracity by expert journalists. The best model reaches a Macro F1 of 49.2%, so the dataset is a challenging testbed.
notes: specific. Names the dataset. Answer is in the abstract of 1909.03242 (26 websites, expert journalists, Macro F1 49.2%); the paper is from 2019.
author: LDN

question: How much of BERT's accuracy does contrastive pruning keep on QQP and MNLI when 97% of the parameters are removed?
reference_answer: With only 3% of the parameters kept (97% sparsity), contrastive pruning (CAP) keeps 99.2% of the original BERT performance on QQP and 96.3% on MNLI.
notes: expert. Names the method (contrastive pruning, CAP). Answer is in the abstract of 2112.07198; the paper is from 2021.
author: LDN

question: For searching legal documents in French, does combining several retrieval models work better than using the best single one?
reference_answer: It depends on the setting. Without in-domain training (zero-shot), fusing different general-purpose models consistently beats a single model, whatever the fusion method. When the models are trained in-domain, fusion generally does worse than the best single system, unless the scores are fused with carefully tuned weights.
notes: plain. Answer is in the abstract of 2409.01357 (French legal hybrid search, zero-shot vs in-domain). Close to our own hybrid retriever, but it is one study on one domain; other papers may report differently (see the pooling rule 9).
author: LDN

question: How can randomly switching off attention heads while training make a speech recognition Transformer better, even though every head is used at test time?
reference_answer: Many attention heads of a trained model are redundant (their attention matrices are close to diagonal). Removing heads at random during training and keeping all of them at test time makes the final model an ensemble of models with different architectures and forces each head to learn useful patterns on its own. It gave consistent gains on Wall Street Journal, AISHELL, Switchboard and AMI.
notes: specific. Names the idea. Answer is in the abstract of 2011.04004; the paper is from 2020.
author: LDN

question: When a language model is asked again and again to improve its own answer without being told what is wrong, what happens over the rounds?
reference_answer: In the study of this intrinsic self-correction, performance improves progressively over the rounds and then converges to a stable level. Consistent instructions reduce the model's uncertainty, which brings both its calibration error and its self-correction performance to a stable state; the authors link this to latent concepts that the instructions activate.
notes: plain. Answer is in the abstract of 2406.02378. The question says "what happens", because the abstract reports convergence, not a reason why improvement stops.
author: LDN

question: How can a game-theoretic rationalization framework stop a toxic-language detector from linking dialect or identity words to toxicity?
reference_answer: Invariant rationalization (InvRat) pairs a rationale generator with a predictor in a game, which rules out spurious correlations between certain syntactic patterns, such as identity mentions or dialect, and the toxicity labels. It gave a lower false positive rate for lexical and dialectal attributes than earlier debiasing methods.
notes: expert. Names the approach by what it does. Answer is in the abstract of 2106.07240; the paper is from 2021.
author: LDN

question: How do SeqXGPT and STADEE differ in the way they detect machine-generated text?
reference_answer: SeqXGPT is built for sentence-level detection: it takes lists of log probabilities from white-box LLMs, treated like waves, and feeds them to convolution and self-attention networks. STADEE combines statistical text features, such as token probability and cumulative probability (to handle nucleus sampling), with a deep classifier, and was tested in-domain, out-of-domain and in the wild.
notes: specific. Names both. Needs both abstracts: 2310.08903 (SeqXGPT) and 2312.01672 (STADEE). Each abstract describes its own method; neither compares the two.
author: LDN

question: How does grouped-query attention speed up a language model differently from letting only the top-k tokens through each layer, as in mixture-of-depths?
reference_answer: Grouped-query attention uses an intermediate number of key-value heads (more than one, fewer than the query heads), so decoding is about as fast as with multi-query attention and quality stays close to multi-head attention; existing multi-head checkpoints can be uptrained to it with about 5% of the original pre-training compute. Mixture-of-depths instead caps the number of tokens that take part in self-attention and the MLP at each layer, chosen by top-k routing, so a forward pass needs a fraction of the FLOPs and sampling steps can be up to 50% faster while matching baseline performance.
notes: specific. Names both. Needs both abstracts: 2305.13245 (GQA) and 2404.02258 (Mixture-of-Depths). Each abstract describes its own method; neither compares the two.
author: LDN

question: Name one way to find out what a language model knows from its internal activations without labels, and one way to judge how reliable its answers are when you only see its outputs.
reference_answer: From the internal activations: an unsupervised method finds a direction in activation space that satisfies logical consistency (a statement and its negation have opposite truth values); across 6 models and 10 question-answering datasets it beat zero-shot accuracy by 4% on average. From outputs only, for a black-box model: a simple measure of the semantic dispersion of the generated answers was a reliable predictor of response quality.
notes: expert. Needs two abstracts: 2212.03827 (latent knowledge from activations) and 2305.19187 (uncertainty for black-box LLMs). Other papers in the full index may also answer (see the pooling rule 9; gs-007 asks about internal states too).
author: LDN

question: In a retrieval-augmented system, is exact nearest-neighbour search worth its cost compared with approximate search, and how can an approximate tree index lose less retrieval quality?
reference_answer: Approximate search speeds up dense retrieval but usually costs retrieval quality; JTR trains a tree-based index and the query encoder jointly with one contrastive loss and gets better retrieval at high efficiency. In RAG pipelines, exact search is expensive but can lower inference time compared with approximate search, because it sends a smaller, more accurate list of documents to the generator at the same end-to-end accuracy.
notes: expert. Needs two abstracts: 2304.11943 (JTR, tree-based index) and 2412.15246 (exact vs approximate retrieval in RAG). Other papers in the full index may also answer (see the pooling rule 9).
author: LDN

question: What happens if the questions use brand names instead?
reference_answer: Accuracy drops consistently, by 1 to 10%, for both open-source and API-based models on MedQA and MedMCQA when brand and generic drug names are swapped. The authors point to contamination of test data in widely used pre-training datasets as a possible source of this fragility.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that the questions are medical benchmark questions and the names are drug names. Answer is in the abstract of 2406.12066.
author: LDN

history.content: How are language models tested on medical knowledge?
They are evaluated on medical benchmarks such as MedQA and MedMCQA.

standalone_query: How does replacing generic drug names with brand names change language model accuracy on medical benchmarks such as MedQA and MedMCQA?

question: Can they be fooled easily?
reference_answer: Yes. The study found that detectors depend on subtle differences such as an extra space, and its SpaceInfi strategy exploits this to evade detection across multiple benchmarks and detectors. The authors give a theoretical explanation for perplexity-based detectors and attribute the evasion of language-model-based detectors to token mutation.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that "they" are detectors of ChatGPT-written text. Answer is in the abstract of 2307.02599.
author: LDN

history.content: How do tools that detect ChatGPT-written text work?
Existing detectors assume there are distributional gaps between human-written and AI-written text, which they find with statistical information or with trained classifiers.

standalone_query: Can detectors of ChatGPT-generated text be evaded easily?

question: How good can it get in a day on one graphics card?
reference_answer: Close to BERT: the authors provide a modified pretraining pipeline with performance close to BERT, and show that even in this constrained setting performance closely follows the scaling laws seen with large compute.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that the topic is training a language model from scratch. Answer is in the abstract of 2212.14034; the abstract does not give a benchmark number.
author: LDN

history.content: Is it realistic for a researcher without a big lab to train a language model from scratch?
Scaling up has made training language models out of reach for most researchers and practitioners.

standalone_query: How well can a transformer language model trained from scratch for one day on a single consumer GPU perform?

question: In one study that gave GPT-4 news headlines published after its knowledge cutoff, how well did the model predict the stock market's first reaction?
reference_answer: About 90% portfolio-day hit rates for the initial, non-tradable reaction. The model's scores also significantly predicted the later drift in prices, especially for small stocks and negative news.
notes: plain. Answer is in the abstract of 2304.07619. The question says "one study" because other papers may test LLMs on financial news (FORMAT.md rule 10).
author: LDN

question: The first broad evaluation of ChatGPT as a zero-shot Text-to-SQL system used how many benchmark datasets, and in which setting did it beat a fine-tuned state-of-the-art model?
reference_answer: It used 12 benchmark datasets. In the ADVETA (RPL) scenario, zero-shot ChatGPT beat the state-of-the-art model fine-tuned on Spider by 4.1%, although overall there was still a gap to the best models.
notes: specific. Aimed at one paper. Both numbers (12 datasets, 4.1%) are in the abstract of 2303.13547.
author: LDN

question: In one study of multilingual instruction tuning, how many multilingual examples added to an English-only tuning set were enough to clearly improve instruction following in other languages?
reference_answer: Only 40 multilingual examples mixed into an English tuning set substantially improved instruction following, both in languages seen and unseen during tuning.
notes: expert. Answer is in the abstract of 2401.01854. The abstract also says that adding 2-4 languages improves cross-lingual generalisation, which is not needed for this answer.
author: LDN

question: According to the gradient entanglement analysis of margin-based alignment losses, why can training make a language model more likely to produce the response it was told to avoid?
reference_answer: Margin-based losses only specify the difference between preferred and dispreferred responses. They couple the change in the preferred probability to the gradient of the dispreferred one and vice versa, which often stops one from rising while the other falls, so both probabilities can increase or decrease together.
notes: expert. Names the analysis. Answer is in the abstract of 2410.13828.
author: LDN

question: In one comparison across nine language models, how did putting distractor options into the prompt change how well the models' stated confidence matched their correctness?
reference_answer: Distractor-augmented prompts substantially reduced miscalibration in that study (ECE reductions up to 90%). Smaller models benefited the most but stayed miscalibrated, while large RLHF-tuned models were better calibrated by default but could be worse on easier questions.
notes: plain. Answer is in the abstract of 2502.11028. The question says "one comparison" because other papers study calibration.
author: LDN

question: How can soft prompts help a LLaMA-7B model that has been compressed with 4-bit quantization and 50% weight pruning to recover its accuracy?
reference_answer: A soft prompt is learned while the compressed model is exposed to the prompt learning process. With this prompt, the 8x compressed model could match its uncompressed counterpart on popular benchmarks.
notes: expert. Names the compression setting. Answer is in the abstract of 2305.11186.
author: LDN

question: How does fine-tuning a translation model with nearest-neighbour statistics differ from kNN-MT with dynamic retrieval in where the nearest-neighbour information is used and what it is meant to achieve?
reference_answer: The first uses statistics from kNN predictions to inform the gradient updates while fine-tuning a translation model (gating, kNN ground-truth probability or reinforcement learning), to gain translation quality over classic fine-tuning. The second keeps an external datastore at translation time and uses a classifier and a timestep-aware threshold to decide when to skip kNN retrieval, to cut the time overhead of retrieving at every step.
notes: expert. Two methods named by what they do. Answers are in the abstracts of 2305.13648 (fine-tuning, up to 1.45 BLEU) and 2406.06073 (skipping retrieval).
author: LDN

question: What problem does the ROPO preference-optimization method address, and how is that different from the problem addressed by self-augmented preference optimization (SAPO)?
reference_answer: ROPO deals with noise in preference data: it down-weights and filters noisy samples during iterative training without external models. SAPO deals with the dependence on static, pre-collected paired preference data: it generates negative responses by self-play and uses an off-policy pipeline with an EMA model and a replay buffer.
notes: specific. Names both methods. Answers are in the abstracts of 2404.04102 and 2405.20830.
author: LDN

question: Name one way to improve a dense retriever using a cross-encoder teacher, and one way to adapt a dense retriever to a new domain when only a short text description of that domain is available.
reference_answer: One way is ADAM, which distills a cross-encoder into the dual-encoder using adaptive dark examples (passages of moderate relevance made by mixing-up and masking) with self-paced distillation. The other is to generate a synthetic document collection, queries and pseudo relevance labels from the domain description and adapt the retriever on that data.
notes: expert. Needs one abstract for each half: 2212.10192 (distillation) and 2307.02740 (adaptation from a domain description). A pipeline for both appears in no single abstract.
author: LDN

question: Name two different ways to reduce overconfidence in language models: one that combines several viewpoints to estimate confidence, and one that passes reasoning from a larger model to a smaller one.
reference_answer: Multi-Perspective Consistency combines insights from within a model and across different models to estimate confidence and mitigate overconfidence. Knowledge transfer uses chain-of-thought reasoning from a big LLM to fine-tune a small LLM so that its predictions are more accurate and its confidence better calibrated.
notes: plain. Needs both abstracts: 2402.11279 (multi-perspective consistency) and 2405.16856 (knowledge transfer).
author: LDN

question: Which two LLM-based Text-to-SQL approaches improve results by retrieving demonstrations with the needed logical operators and by handling the wide tables of financial databases, and what does each report?
reference_answer: PURPLE retrieves demonstrations that contain the required logical operator composition and reports 80.5% exact-set match and 87.8% execution match on the Spider validation set. FinSQL targets financial databases with prompt construction, parameter-efficient fine-tuning and output calibration, introduces the BULL benchmark, and reports up to 36.64% improvement in few-shot cross-database transfer.
notes: specific. Needs both abstracts: 2403.20014 (PURPLE) and 2401.10506 (FinSQL).
author: LDN

question: Name one cause of a knowledge-edited language model collapsing after a single ROME edit, and one way edited models still fail on reasoning questions. How was each addressed?
reference_answer: Collapse comes from inconsistent handling of prefixed and unprefixed keys, which can make a denominator very small and the parameter update very large; the fix is to use prefixed keys consistently. On reasoning questions, edited models tend to keep outdated answers; the DISCO decoding strategy amplifies the difference between the edited and the original model's token predictions to reduce this.
notes: expert. Needs both abstracts: 2406.11263 (collapse) and 2406.02882 (outdated issue).

question: Does picking the languages carefully always work better than picking them at random?
reference_answer: No. In that study no universal language-selection strategy emerged: performance depended strongly on the task and the model, and adding more languages beyond a modest threshold made results worse.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that the topic is choosing languages for multilingual instruction tuning. Answer is in the abstract of 2410.07809.

question: What if a person edits the text afterwards?
reference_answer: Human edits dilute the watermark signal and degrade existing detectors. A truncated goodness-of-fit test (Tr-GoF) was proposed to detect watermarked text under edits, and it is shown to be optimal for the Gumbel-max watermark in certain regimes, unlike sum-based rules.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that the topic is watermark detection in AI-written text. Answer is in the abstract of 2411.13868.
author: LDN

history.content: How can I tell whether a text was written by an AI?
One approach is to check for a statistical watermark that the language model embedded while generating the text.

standalone_query: How can a watermark in LLM-generated text still be detected after a human has edited the text?

question: Is there a way for it to check its own answer and look things up again?
reference_answer: Yes: the GrowOVER authors propose a training-free retrieval-interactive framework in which the language model evaluates and reflects on its answer and re-retrieves when needed. It performs comparably to or better than continuously trained language models on their benchmarks.
notes: plain. Needs the history to know that the topic is retrieval-augmented models answering about knowledge that changed. Answer is in the abstract of 2406.05606.
author: LDN

history.content: Why do retrieval-augmented language models sometimes give outdated answers?
Knowledge keeps changing, and the model or its document store may not have been updated.

standalone_query: How can a retrieval-augmented language model use self-reflection and re-retrieval to handle knowledge that has changed or was not in its training data?
